claims.text: The baseline RHEA is composed primarily of high-melting-point elements such as Nb, Mo, Ta, and W.
The baseline RHEA contains no significant lightweight-alloying additions.
The proposed intervention is addition of 1–3 at.% Al to the baseline RHEA.
The Al addition will form nanoscale Al-rich intermetallic precipitates.
The Al-rich precipitates will be coherent with the matrix.
The Al-rich precipitates will remain stable at elevated temperature.
Coherent Al-rich precipitates will impede high-temperature dislocation glide.
Impeded dislocation motion will enhance high-temperature yield strength.
Impeded dislocation motion will improve creep resistance.
Limiting Al to 1–3 at.% will prevent the formation of large brittle phases.
Limiting Al to 1–3 at.% will preserve room-temperature ductility.
The Al-added alloy will have at least 15% greater high-temperature yield strength than the Al-free baseline.
The Al-added alloy will exhibit a lower creep rate than the Al-free baseline.
The density increase caused by Al addition will be less than 5% relative to the baseline.
The Al addition will cause negligible changes in room-temperature mechanical properties.
The predicted high-temperature benefits should hold under tensile and creep loading at approximately 800–1000°C.
Coarse or brittle phase formation, phase segregation, or rapid precipitate coarsening could prevent the predicted benefits.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis calls the addition a 'small volume fraction' but quantifies it in atomic percent; volume fraction and atomic fraction are distinct composition measures.
